questions.q: Why is mean latency described as potentially the most misleading single number to report for a trading system?
options: The mean can look consistently fast even when a rare but real tail of much slower samples exists, since averaging spreads that tail's cost across every sample
The mean is mathematically impossible to compute for latency data
The mean is always higher than every individual sample
Trading systems never experience latency variance, making the mean always accurate
questions.explain: A low mean can hide a real tail of slow outliers -- averaging dilutes the rare slow samples' impact on the reported number, even though those slow samples still happen regularly in a high-volume system.

questions.q: What does 'p99' mean as a latency statistic?
options: 99% of recorded samples were at or below this value -- only 1% were slower
The 99th sample recorded, in chronological order
99% of all possible latencies, a theoretical upper bound
The average of the slowest 99 samples
questions.explain: A percentile reports what fraction of samples fall at or below a given value -- p99 specifically means only 1% of samples were slower than the reported number.

questions.q: In the worked example (n=10,000, mean=10.55us, p50=9.03us, p99=12.85us, p99.9=228.66us), why is p99.9 the number that actually exposes the tail event?
options: The tail event affected only 1% of samples, so it doesn't show up until you look past p99 -- p99.9 is the first percentile fine-grained enough to reveal it
p99.9 is simply a typo or rounding artifact and shouldn't be trusted
Mean, p50, and p99 are all equally capable of showing the tail event
p99.9 measures something completely unrelated to the other percentiles
questions.explain: Since the tail event hit about 1% of samples, p99 sits right at the edge of catching it and p99.9 is well past that edge -- which is exactly why it jumps to over 20x the mean while the other reported numbers look unremarkable.

questions.q: What is the key difference between latency and throughput as performance metrics?
options: Latency asks how long one operation takes; throughput asks how many operations complete per unit time -- and optimizing one can hurt the other
Latency and throughput are two names for the exact same measurement
Throughput only applies to networking code, never to local computation
Latency can only be measured in nanoseconds, while throughput can only be measured in seconds
questions.explain: They answer genuinely different questions, and batching (which improves throughput) can directly hurt the latency of any individual operation stuck waiting in that batch -- the same tension as Nagle's algorithm from Lesson 39.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say reporting the wrong metric (e.g., throughput for a latency-critical order-entry path) 'actively hides' whether a system is doing its job well?
options: A system can have excellent throughput while still having unacceptable tail latency on individual time-critical operations, so the 'good' throughput number masks the actual problem that matters for that use case
Throughput and latency numbers are always identical, so it doesn't matter which is reported
Reporting throughput is always wrong in every context
There is no real difference between reporting the two metrics
questions.explain: Which metric matters depends on the system's actual job -- an order-entry path cares about individual latency, not aggregate throughput, so a throughput number can look great while hiding exactly the tail-latency problem that matters there.
